exercise.title: Why is constant-velocity displacement the area of a rectangle?

statement.p: If velocity is constantly 60 miles per hour for 3 hours, the displacement is 180 miles, which is also the area of a rectangle of height 60 and width 3. In your own words, why do the units already force that product to be a distance, and why is the same idea waiting inside a velocity graph?

hint.p: Signed displacement equals constant velocity times elapsed time. Distance traveled equals speed times elapsed time. On the graph, height times width is the corresponding product.

subsection.title: Piecewise constant velocity
subsection.p: Real velocity is rarely constant for a whole trip. The next simplest case is piecewise constant velocity: constant for a while, then another constant, then another. This idealized model has instantaneous velocity changes. At each jump the position is continuous but has no two-sided derivative; the velocity formula describes the motion away from those instants.

exercise.title: Why do we pretend velocity is constant on short intervals?

statement.p: When velocity changes, we sample it, build rectangles, and add. In your own words, why is each product sampled velocity times time width a piece of displacement, and why do shorter intervals usually make the estimate more trustworthy?

hint.p: On sufficiently short intervals, slowly varying velocity is approximated by a constant. Summing the corresponding displacements estimates the total displacement.

subsection.title: Signed displacement versus total distance
subsection.p: Velocity has a sign. Positive velocity means motion in the positive direction. Negative velocity means motion in the negative direction.
That creates two different questions.

p.me: \text{What is the net change in position?}

subsection.p: The first question asks for signed displacement. The second asks for total distance traveled.

exercise.title: Why are signed displacement and total distance different questions?

statement.p: Positive velocity and negative velocity contribute with opposite signs to net change of position, but total distance traveled adds the sizes of the pieces. In your own words, why can a trip end near its starting point after covering a large distance, and which accumulation uses |v(t)|?

hint.p: Displacement accumulates velocity, including backward motion as negative. Distance traveled accumulates speed, so cancellation is removed.
